description: The best team in the universe. Not accepting applications unless plant music excites you.
summary:
You are alone in orbit. The radio crackles. Something down there is broadcasting.
Terra Sonica is a radio you tune from a spacecraft cockpit. Every station is a real NASA
Earth dataset, turned into music and shown on an interactive 3D globe through the window that you can orbit, zoom and read. The data writes the notes; we gave them their sound. The five stations follow the warmth at the height of your face, the nitrogen oxides cities breathe out, the winds that carry everything, the fine particles you breathe without seeing, and 143 years of a planet slowly leaving “normal” behind.

The challenge asked for Earth data that is multi-sensory and accessible. Most climate data lives in colour maps. People who can’t see them are shut out, and most people who can see them glance and move on. Terra Sonica offers three ways in: you hear it, you see it move, and it speaks to you. Every value on the planet can be read aloud. The console lights pulse with the music for players who can’t hear it. Everything works from the keyboard.

It matters because data only changes minds when people stay with it long enough to feel it. We wanted the planet to stop being a chart and become a voice.
details:
What it does

Terra Sonica puts you in the pilot’s seat of a spacecraft in geostationary orbit, 36,000 km above Earth. The ship’s radio picks up five stations. Each one is a NASA Scientific Visualization Studio record:

Earth's Crust: air temperature 2 m above the ground, hour by hour. It sounds warm and full: a steady, wide pulse.

Acid Lover: nitrogen oxides (NO and NO2) near the ground. It sounds low and relentless: a hum that never switches off.

Fūjin: wind speed 10 m above the surface. It sounds deep and still, then gathers like a storm.

Nanoair: fine particles (PM2.5) near the ground. It sounds bright, fine and restless.

Anything but Albus: temperature anomalies, 1880 to 2023. It sounds deep and dark, growing brighter as the decades warm.

When you tune in:

  • The globe outside your window shows that station’s data, animated in sync with the music.
  • The planet’s glow and the cockpit lights take the station’s colour.
  • A large date on the glass and a timeline below tell you exactly when you are.

You can drag the planet to orbit it, scroll to dive closer, and point anywhere to read an estimate of the value there, such as “Beijing, nitrogen oxides about 11 ppbv”. The bottom-left window always shows NASA’s original visualization, with its record number, so the source is never hidden.

Every name means something:

  • Earth’s Crust is the thin layer of air where we actually live.
  • Acid Lover is for the gases that turn into acid rain.
  • Fūjin is the Japanese god who carries the winds in a bag.
  • Nanoair is for the particles too fine to see.
  • Anything but Albus: albus is Latin for white, and on NASA’s map white means normal.

Who it is for, and how it is accessible

We designed for people who are usually left out of data, from the first prototype on:

  • Blind and low-vision players:
    • Every control works from the keyboard.
    • Values are spoken on request (V).
    • Each station’s story can be narrated (N).
    • Screen readers receive every announcement.
    • The console lights pulse with the music, low notes on the left and high notes on the right. They work even with the sound muted.
    • Each station describes the feel of its music in words.
    • Nothing ever flashes.
    • Motion is reduced when the system asks for it.
  • Everyone: a “how to play” guide opens on the first visit and is always one key (H) away.

How we made it: our process

  1. A record player for the planet. It started as a browser app where every NASA dataset was a vinyl record. A scanline swept the map from west to east and played it: value became pitch, longitude moved the sound from ear to ear, latitude chose the instrument. On our first tests we found it chaotic, so we rebuilt the sound around calm, slow chords. Accessibility was there from day one.
  2. A room that is the planet. Inspired by teamLab, we envisioned the project as an immersive installation and built a TouchDesigner bridge for it. It became our long-term vision (see Next steps below).
    • Value readback: the colour under the cursor is matched against NASA’s own colour bars to estimate the real number.
    • Light organ: the cockpit lamps play along with the music.
    • Narration: station stories read aloud, but only when the player asks, so it never becomes noise.
    • Scientific notation: formulas like NO₂ and PM₂.₅ written properly, with the wording NASA uses.
  3. Open to everyone. Terra Sonica runs in any modern browser from a single link. There’s nothing to install, and an offline version exists for exhibitions.

How it works

  • The NASA frames are processed into clean image sequences and drawn onto a WebGL globe.
  • Each station’s music drives the animation clock, so sound and image stay in step, including when you pause.
  • Values are read by matching colours against NASA’s published colour bars.
  • The light organ splits the live music into six frequency bands.

What we hope to achieve

We hope people stop and listen. That a blind student can hear where the air is dirtiest, a player with hearing difficulties can watch the music move across the console, and someone who has never read a climate chart can feel the white of “normal” slowly disappear. We want data to be something you experience, not something you skip.

See all our project's materials here:)

Tools

  • Code: HTML, CSS, JavaScript; three.js (WebGL); Web Audio API; Tone.js (first prototype); globe.gl (standalone globes).
  • Data and media processing: Python (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, Pillow, Matplotlib, librosa), Tesseract OCR, Node.js, ffmpeg.
  • Testing: Playwright, plus manual testing in Firefox and Chrome.
  • Music: Python scripts that turn each video into MIDI, then Logic Pro (Alchemy synthesizer, ChromaVerb, Channel EQ, Mastering Assistant).
  • Visuals: Higgsfield (cockpit artwork, intro), After Effects and Kapwing (intro edit), Canva (UI).
  • Hosting: GitHub Pages.
  • Planned installation: TouchDesigner.

Next steps: how we imagine Terra Sonica evolving

The game is the first step. Our vision is a room that is the planet.

The installation:

  • The world map wraps around four walls, so the room becomes the full circle of the Earth.
  • The music travels around visitors through a ring of speakers, following the data from west to east.
  • The Arctic sits near the ceiling and Antarctica near the floor.
  • Bodies as the cursor: a depth camera follows visitors. Wherever someone stands, that place on Earth plays and lights up, so two people across the room can hear their two places talk.
  • The past under your feet: the present plays on the walls while the past is projected on the floor. Visitors stand on the old Earth while the new one surrounds them.

Built for every body:

  • a vibrating floor or bench for visitors with hearing difficulties
  • a tactile map and headphones with narration for blind visitors
  • quiet hours, and no flashing light, ever

One data stream, every sense: the same stream drives the room, the web game and phone vibration, so a visitor listening at home hears exactly what the wall shows.

Along the way:

  • more stations: ozone, sea ice, wildfires, rainfall
  • listening tests with blind and low-vision listeners
  • live data that updates as NASA publishes it
  • versions in more languages, starting with Greek
  • a mobile version

Use of Artificial Intelligence

The concept, the station choices and names, the visual direction and the sound of the music are ours; the notes themselves come from NASA’s data.

Claude (Anthropic, large language model):

  • writing and debugging the code
  • writing the Python scripts that turn the data into MIDI
  • processing NASA’s frames, and syncing them to our music
  • building the colour-to-value readback
  • analysing our tracks to help describe their mood in words
  • automated testing
  • drafting the in-game texts, this description and the technical documentation from our direction and NASA’s own pages; we reviewed and chose every text
  • suggesting features, some of which we chose to build (the light organ and the value readback)

ChatGPT (OpenAI, large language model): turning NASA’s five videos into grid data, meaning extracting the frames, sampling them on a 5° grid, and writing the scripts for that step.

Higgsfield (image and video generation): the cockpit artwork and the intro film, which we edited in After Effects and Kapwing. Both carry a visible ✦AI mark in the game.

Disclosures: the code, texts, artwork and intro film are acknowledged in the game’s metadata and in the repository README.

NASA Data

The five videos come from NASA’s Earth Information Center collection, published by the NASA Scientific Visualization Studio:

  • SVS 5147: GEOS-FP Near-Surface Temperature
  • SVS 5148: GEOS-FP Near-Surface Wind Speed
  • SVS 5151: Particulate Matter (PM) 2.5, GEOS-CF
  • SVS 5154: Nitrogen Oxides (NOₓ), GEOS-CF
  • SVS 5207: Global Temperature Anomalies 1880 to 2023, GISTEMP

How we used it: each video’s frames were sampled into data and turned into music, cleaned and wrapped onto the globe, and read back as values through NASA’s own colour bars. The original frames play unaltered in the source window.

Organisations: NASA Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) and NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS). Visualizer of the four GMAO records: Joseph V. Ardizzone (NASA/GSFC).

Earth imagery: NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble.

First prototype: NASA GIBS imagery and the GISTEMP v4 record.

Space Agency Partner Data and Other References

  • Space Agency Partner data: none used.
  • Data in the first prototype only: NOAA Mauna Loa CO₂ record; NSIDC Sea Ice Index.
  • Map outlines: Natural Earth land outlines (public domain), via world-atlas.
  • Code libraries: three.js (MIT), globe.gl (MIT), Tone.js (MIT).
  • Font: JetBrains Mono (SIL Open Font License).
  • Tools: Python (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, Pillow, Matplotlib, librosa), Tesseract OCR, ffmpeg, Node.js, Logic Pro (Alchemy, ChromaVerb, Channel EQ, Mastering Assistant), Playwright, GitHub Pages, Higgsfield, After Effects, Kapwing, Canva, Claude, ChatGPT.
  • References for the texts: NASA’s SVS pages, and NASA’s January 2024 release confirming 2023 as the warmest year on record.
